name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
summary: Retrograde flow of gastric contents causing troublesome symptoms and/or mucosal injury. The most common acid-related condition in ambulatory care.
pathophysiology: Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations (tLESRs) allow reflux of acid and pepsin; mucosal defense fails with prolonged exposure. Risk factors include obesity, hiatus hernia, and pregnancy. Complications: erosive esophagitis, stricture, Barrett esophagus, aspiration.
diagnosis: Typical symptoms (heartburn, regurgitation) justify an empiric trial; endoscopy when alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, anemia) or refractory symptoms are present.

guidelines.rec: An 8-week trial of a standard-dose PPI before the first meal is the empiric therapy of choice for typical GERD.
PPIs are the most effective agents for healing erosive esophagitis and maintaining remission.
Lifestyle modification (weight loss, head-of-bed elevation, avoiding late meals) complements but does not replace pharmacotherapy.
Refractory GERD (no response to adequate PPI) warrants adherence/timing review before escalating; consider PCABs or pH-impedance testing referral.

treatmentTiers.label: Standard PPI 30–60 min before breakfast
H2-receptor antagonist (as-needed milder disease), antacids/alginate for breakthrough
Dual delayed-release PPI or PCAB; reconsider adherence first

refs.label: ACG Clinical Guideline on GERD Management

provenance.notes: Guideline statements distilled from ACG clinical guidelines; grades reflect the published guideline ratings.

name: Peptic ulcer disease
summary: Disruption of the gastroduodenal mucosa exceeding the muscularis mucosae — most often from H. pylori infection or NSAID use.
pathophysiology: Imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori virulence) and mucosal defense. H. pylori colonizes the antral mucosa and impairs somatostatin/acid feedback; NSAIDs suppress mucosal prostaglandins. Complications: bleeding, perforation, gastric outlet obstruction.
diagnosis: Endoscopy is the gold standard; non-invasive H. pylori testing (urea breath test, stool antigen) for young patients without alarm features.

guidelines.rec: Test for H. pylori in all patients with active or past peptic ulcer disease; treat if positive, with post-treatment confirmation.
Eradication therapy: clarithromycin triple therapy where resistance <15%, otherwise bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline) for 14 days.
NSAID-associated ulcers: stop the NSAID if possible; PPI co-therapy for the duration if it must continue.
H. pylori-negative, NSAID-negative ulcers should raise suspicion for other causes (Zollinger–Ellison, Crohn, malignancy).

treatmentTiers.label: PPI + antibiotics (clarithromycin triple or bismuth quadruple), 10–14 days
PPI once daily for 4–8 weeks; longer for large/complicated ulcers
PPI co-therapy for continuing NSAID users at risk

name: Acne vulgaris
summary: Chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit — the most common skin condition treated by physicians.
pathophysiology: Four interacting mechanisms: follicular hyperkeratinization, increased sebum production, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and inflammation. Androgens drive sebocyte activity. Scarring risk tracks disease severity and duration.
diagnosis: Clinical. Classify by predominant lesion type (comedonal, inflammatory, nodulocystic) and severity to choose therapy.

guidelines.rec: Combination topical therapy (retinoid + benzoyl peroxide) is the preferred backbone for mild-to-moderate acne.
Topical retinoids are first-line for comedonal acne and as maintenance.
Topical antibiotics should be combined with benzoyl peroxide to limit resistance and should not be used as monotherapy.
Systemic isotretinoin is the most effective therapy for severe or scarring acne; pregnancy prevention is mandatory.

treatmentTiers.label: Topical retinoid monotherapy, introduced gradually
Topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide combination (± topical antibiotic bridged with BPO)
Add time-limited oral antibiotic (tetracycline class) as bridge; plan topical maintenance after
Isotretinoin under specialist care (iPLEDGE-style pregnancy prevention)

name: Rosacea
summary: Chronic inflammatory facial dermatosis with erythema, papulopustules, and telangiectasia; subtype-driven management.
pathophysiology: Multifactorial: dysregulation of innate immunity (cathelicidin peptides), Demodex folliculorum overgrowth, neurovascular hyperreactivity, and UV exposure. Triggers (heat, alcohol, spicy food) provoke flushing.
diagnosis: Clinical, based on phenotype: erythematotelangiectatic (ETR), papulopustular (PPR), phymatous, ocular.

guidelines.rec: Topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin are effective for papulopustular rosacea.
Subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline (40 mg) is effective and minimizes antibiotic resistance pressure.
Brimonidine or oxymetazoline topical agents reduce persistent facial erythema.

treatmentTiers.label: Topical azelaic acid or metronidazole; add subantimicrobial doxycycline for moderate severity
Vasoconstrictor topicals (brimonidine/oxymetazoline) or laser for telangiectasia

name: Psoriasis
summary: Immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease driven by IL-23/Th17 axis; plaque psoriasis is the most common form.
pathophysiology: IL-23 → Th17 differentiation → IL-17A drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation and neutrophil recruitment. Genetic predisposition (HLA-Cw6), triggers include infection, stress, drugs.
diagnosis: Clinical (sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale); guttate, inverse, pustular, and erythrodermic variants exist.

guidelines.rec: Topical corticosteroids ± vitamin D analogs are first-line for mild plaque psoriasis.
Phototherapy (narrowband UVB) is effective for moderate disease.
Biologics targeting TNF, IL-17, IL-23 are highly effective for moderate-to-severe disease.

treatmentTiers.label: Topical corticosteroid ± vitamin D analog
Phototherapy or systemic (methotrexate, apremilast)
Biologic therapy (IL-17/IL-23/TNF inhibitors)

name: Hypertension
summary: Sustained elevation of arterial pressure; the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease worldwide.
pathophysiology: Chronic elevation of systemic vascular resistance; contributions from sodium handling (kidney), RAAS activation, sympathetic tone, and arterial stiffness. Target-organ damage: heart, brain, kidneys, eyes.
diagnosis: Office BP ≥130/80 mmHg (ACC/AHA 2017) confirmed on repeated measurement; out-of-office confirmation (ABPM/home) recommended.

guidelines.rec: Initiate pharmacotherapy at BP ≥130/80 mmHg with ASCVD risk ≥10%, or ≥140/90 regardless of risk.
First-line classes: thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and calcium channel blockers — alone or in combination.
Beta-blockers are not first-line unless a compelling indication (CAD, HFrEF, arrhythmia) exists.
Two-drug combination (often ACEi/ARB + CCB or thiazide) for stage 2 hypertension or ≥20/10 mmHg above goal.

treatmentTiers.label: ACE inhibitor or ARB, CCB, or thiazide — alone or combined
Beta-blocker for CAD/HF; ACEi/ARB for diabetes/CKD; consider mineralocorticoid antagonist for resistant HTN

refs.label: 2017 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults

name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
summary: Progressive disorder of insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency; management is individualized around glycemia, weight, and cardiovascular risk.
pathophysiology: Peripheral insulin resistance plus progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction. Visceral adiposity drives ectopic lipid accumulation and inflammation. Complications: microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular (ASCVD).
diagnosis: A1c ≥6.5%, fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, 2-h OGTT ≥200 mg/dL, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms.

guidelines.rec: Metformin is the preferred initial agent for most people with T2DM (also consider earlier combination therapy).
In patients with ASCVD, HF, or CKD, an SGLT2 inhibitor and/or GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven benefit is recommended regardless of A1c.
GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists are preferred where weight loss is a goal.
Individualize glycemic targets (A1c <7% for most non-pregnant adults; less stringent for frailty/hypoglycemia risk).

treatmentTiers.label: Metformin + lifestyle (or earlier combination for high A1c)
Add SGLT2 inhibitor (HF/CKD) and/or GLP-1 RA (ASCVD) with proven benefit
Basal insulin when catabolic symptoms or A1c very high, or when other agents insufficient

name: Asthma
summary: Chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
pathophysiology: Type-2 inflammation (IL-4/IL-5/IL-13) drives eosinophilia, mucus hypersecretion, and airway remodeling. Triggers: allergens, viruses, exercise, irritants. Diagnosis requires variable expiratory airflow limitation (spirometry).
diagnosis: Symptoms (wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough) + documented variable airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC ratio <0.7 with bronchodilator response or PEF variability).

guidelines.rec: Preferred: as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol for mild asthma (Track 1); SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended for adolescents/adults.
Controller therapy is ICS-based at every step; add LABA for moderate–severe disease (ICS–formoterol maintenance and reliever — MART).
Add-on options at higher steps: long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA), biologics for severe type-2 asthma.

treatmentTiers.label: As-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (preferred) or low-dose ICS maintenance
ICS–LABA maintenance and reliever (MART) or medium-dose ICS–LABA
High-dose ICS–LABA + LAMA; consider biologics (anti-IgE/IL-5/IL-4Ra) and sputum-guided care

refs.label: GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention

name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
summary: Preventable and treatable lung disease characterized by persistent airflow limitation, usually progressive.
pathophysiology: Smoke/inhalant exposure → chronic inflammation, protease–antiprotease imbalance, oxidative stress; emphysema (alveolar destruction) + chronic bronchitis (mucus hypersecretion). Exacerbations accelerate decline.
diagnosis: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 confirms persistent obstruction in the right clinical context.

guidelines.rec: Smoking cessation is the single most effective intervention; vaccinate against influenza, pneumococcus, RSV, and COVID-19.
Group E (high exacerbation risk): LAMA + LABA, with ICS added for eosinophil-guided benefit.
SABA/SAMA as needed for all groups; LAMA preferred over LABA for monotherapy.

treatmentTiers.label: Bronchodilator as needed (SABA or SAMA)
LAMA or LABA maintenance
LAMA + LABA; add ICS with eosinophilia (blood eos ≥300)

refs.label: GOLD 2024 Global Strategy for Prevention, Diagnosis and Management of COPD

name: Community-acquired pneumonia
summary: Acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired outside healthcare settings.
pathophysiology: Aspiration of oropharyngeal flora or inhalation of aerosolized pathogens; Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the most common bacterial cause. Impaired host defenses, smoking, and age increase risk.
diagnosis: Clinical (fever, cough, sputum, focal signs) + new infiltrate on imaging; severity scores (CURB-65/PSI) guide site of care.

guidelines.rec: Outpatient, previously healthy, no resistance risk: amoxicillin or doxycycline.
Outpatient with comorbidities or recent antibiotics: amoxicillin–clavulanate or cephalosporin + macrolide, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy.
Empiric coverage must include atypical pathogens (Legionella, Mycoplasma) in most settings.

treatmentTiers.label: Amoxicillin 1 g TID or doxycycline 100 mg BID × 5 days
Amox-clav ± macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone
Beta-lactam + macrolide (preferred) or respiratory fluoroquinolone

refs.label: IDSA/ATS 2019 Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia
